Image Processing · Lab 05 · Material

Histograms and Tonal Adjustments

MaterialPracticeQuiz

Learn to read an image’s tonal distribution and make deliberate adjustments. Compare a book, a tea mug and a small note as you explore which details become clearer and which disappear.

What you will learn

  • Read histograms without confusing counts with spatial positions.
  • Apply brightness, contrast and power curves with explicit numeric ranges.
  • Compare global equalization with local contrast adjustment.
  • Inspect color and detail before adopting a preprocessing rule.

Before this lab: RGB arrays, floating-point conversion and image display.

In this lab

  1. Channel histograms
  2. Distributions and spatial information
  3. Brightness offsets and clipping
  4. Contrast around a pivot
  5. Power curves and gamma convention
  6. Global histogram equalization
  7. Local contrast with CLAHE
  8. Lightness adjustments and color tradeoffs

Prepare your notebook

Use a Python notebook with OpenCV, Pillow, NumPy and Matplotlib. Run the setup once, then run the guided blocks in order. The copy button selects only the code.

The examples were checked with OpenCV 4.13, Pillow 12.3, NumPy 2.2 and Matplotlib 3.11. The repository’s Python requirements list the versions. These pages and images open offline; running the code requires the Python libraries.

Run setup once, then the teaching tasks in order. Each practice or coding-quiz solution must also run after setup alone. Images are locally drawn examples, not photographs.

Python · shared setup
import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw
cv2.setNumThreads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(205)
# Draw a textured desk with printed detail; all returned arrays are RGB uint8.
def draw_scene(seed=1, kind='both'):
    generator = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    h, w = 128, 160
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:h, :w]
    grain = 4 * np.sin(yy * 0.8 + xx * 0.04) + generator.normal(0, 1.2, (h, w))
    base = 145 + 22 * xx / w + grain
    rgb = np.stack([base + 18, base + 2, base - 15], axis=-1)
    canvas = Image.fromarray(np.clip(np.rint(rgb), 0, 255).astype('uint8'))
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(canvas)
    if kind in ('both', 'book'):
        draw.rectangle((10, 17, 72, 98), fill=(35, 64, 105), outline=(15, 30, 52), width=2)
        draw.rectangle((10, 17, 18, 98), fill=(23, 42, 69))
        draw.text((24, 25), 'NOTES', fill=(240, 232, 201))
        for y in range(49, 85, 5):
            draw.line((25, y, 62, y), fill=(94, 128, 153), width=1)
        for y in range(90, 97, 2):
            draw.line((20, y, 70, y), fill=(221, 217, 190), width=1)
    if kind in ('both', 'mug'):
        draw.ellipse((117, 48, 149, 84), outline=(235, 229, 205), width=6)
        draw.rounded_rectangle((89, 39, 127, 100), radius=7, fill=(223, 219, 199), outline=(116, 111, 97), width=2)
        draw.ellipse((89, 32, 127, 49), fill=(243, 235, 205), outline=(83, 73, 58), width=2)
        draw.ellipse((94, 36, 122, 45), fill=(73, 45, 29))
        draw.line((96, 55, 96, 90), fill=(247, 244, 227), width=2)
        draw.text((101, 68), 'TEA', fill=(76, 103, 111))
    draw.rectangle((77, 105, 152, 124), fill=(237, 215, 119), outline=(148, 119, 62))
    draw.text((82, 109), 'tea 4pm', fill=(50, 47, 34))
    return np.asarray(canvas).copy()
clean_rgb = draw_scene(1)

The image comparisons below come from the guided code. Use their captions and shared display scales to compare each change.

Guided task 01

Channel histograms

A histogram counts how often values fall into bins. For an RGB uint8 image, one histogram per channel can use 256 bins covering the integers zero through 255. Each channel contains height times width samples, so each channel histogram must sum to that count. A large peak indicates a common value or range; it does not identify an object or reveal where those pixels are located.

The desk background occupies much of this drawing, so it can dominate the distribution even when the small note is the useful target. Inspect the image beside the counts rather than judging exposure from the tallest bar alone. Different scenes naturally have different distributions, and a dark object need not be an incorrectly exposed object. We plot raw counts with common axes for the three channels. Converting those counts to proportions would support comparisons between images of different sizes, but would still discard spatial arrangement. A histogram therefore complements the picture; it cannot replace a check of whether the relevant text, outline or color remains visible.

Try it

  1. Count each RGB channel with 256 bins.
  2. Check that every channel count sums to the image area.
  3. Compare the dominant values with large regions of the desk.
Python · run in order
histograms = np.stack([np.bincount(clean_rgb[..., c].ravel(), minlength=256) for c in range(3)])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(clean_rgb)
axes[0].set_title('Desk and small printed details')
axes[0].axis('off')
for values, color, name in zip(histograms, ['red', 'green', 'blue'], ['R', 'G', 'B']):
    axes[1].plot(np.arange(256), values, color=color, label=name)
axes[1].set(xlabel='Stored channel value', ylabel='Pixel count', xlim=(0,255), title='One histogram per channel')
axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout()
print('Channel sample counts:', histograms.sum(axis=1))

Read the result

The dominant table colors can produce larger peaks than the note or mug. A small feature can matter to a task even when it contributes few histogram samples.

Change and compare

  • Count only the note crop and compare its distribution.
  • Divide each histogram by its total to display proportions.

Guided task 02

Distributions and spatial information

Two images can have identical histograms and very different content. Reversing the order of pixel rows preserves the number of occurrences of every value while moving the evidence to different positions. This is a useful reminder that histogram agreement does not establish visual equivalence, correct orientation or annotation alignment. A classifier or text reader sees spatial structure as well as values.

Here we convert the RGB desk to a grayscale intensity image using an explicitly named RGB conversion, then flip its rows. This conversion uses weighted encoded color values; it is not a direct measurement of physical illumination. Count both images and calculate the cumulative distribution of the original. The cumulative value at intensity k is the fraction of stored samples at or below k. It starts at the fraction in the first bin and reaches one at the last bin. A cumulative curve can support threshold or percentile reasoning, but cannot tell you whether the upside-down word is still appropriate for a reading label. Keep the coordinate task separate from the distribution task.

Try it

  1. Create grayscale values with COLOR_RGB2GRAY.
  2. Reverse the rows and compare the two count arrays.
  3. Read the cumulative fraction while inspecting both spatial layouts.
Python · run in order
gray = cv2.cvtColor(clean_rgb, cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)
upside_down = gray[::-1].copy()
counts = np.bincount(gray.ravel(), minlength=256)
flipped_counts = np.bincount(upside_down.ravel(), minlength=256)
cdf = np.cumsum(counts) / gray.size
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(gray, cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=255)
axes[0].set_title('Grayscale desk')
axes[1].imshow(upside_down, cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=255)
axes[1].set_title('Same histogram, moved pixels')
for ax in axes[:2]: ax.axis('off')
axes[2].plot(np.arange(256), cdf)
axes[2].set(xlabel='Intensity', ylabel='Fraction at or below', ylim=(0,1), xlim=(0,255), title='Cumulative distribution')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The two pictures have equal counts, yet the printed labels face different directions. The cumulative curve is monotonic because it accumulates nonnegative counts.

Change and compare

  • Reverse columns instead and verify that counts still agree.
  • Find the first intensity where the cumulative fraction reaches one half.

Guided task 03

Brightness offsets and clipping

An additive brightness rule shifts stored channel values by a constant. In this task the offset has units on the zero-to-255 encoded scale. Add it in floating point so values outside the valid range remain visible to the calculation. Only then count out-of-range values, clip to the storage interval, round, and convert to uint8. Adding directly in unsigned storage could wrap instead of producing the intended clipped result.

Clipping is many-to-one: several values above the upper limit all become 255. Once those distinct highlights are merged, subtracting the offset cannot recover them. The same issue applies to dark values clipped to zero. Measure the fraction of channel samples that the unbounded calculation would push outside the interval. This is not the same as counting pixels with any clipped channel, and it is not a probability that a classification label is wrong. Compare the bright mug rim and the dark book cover alongside the fraction. Brightening encoded RGB values is a simple appearance adjustment, not a physically calibrated increase in scene lighting.

Try it

  1. Apply offsets of minus 45 and plus 45 in float32.
  2. Measure clipping before limiting the values.
  3. Compare preserved detail at the same display size.
Python · run in order
offsets = [-45.0, 45.0]
shifted, clipped_fractions = [], []
for offset in offsets:
    raw = clean_rgb.astype(np.float32) + offset
    clipped_fractions.append(float(np.mean((raw < 0) | (raw > 255))))
    shifted.append(np.rint(np.clip(raw, 0, 255)).astype(np.uint8))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
for ax, image, title in zip(axes, [clean_rgb]+shifted, ['Original']+[f'Offset {o:+.0f}: clipped {f:.1%}' for o,f in zip(offsets,clipped_fractions)]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis('off')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Look for values that merge into flat highlights or shadows. The reported percentage describes clipped channel samples, so a pixel may contribute one, two or three samples.

Change and compare

  • Try a smaller offset and inspect the note text.
  • Compute the fraction of pixels with at least one out-of-range channel.

Guided task 04

Contrast around a pivot

A contrast factor describes how far values move from a chosen pivot. We use output = pivot + factor times (input minus pivot), with pivot 127.5 on the zero-to-255 scale. A factor below one pulls values toward mid-gray. A factor above one pushes them away, and can drive them beyond the allowed range. The pivot is part of the definition; another pivot can give another image even with the same factor.

Before clipping, a positive factor preserves the ordering of scalar values. It does not guarantee preservation of color relationships or all visible detail after independently changing the channels. A high factor can merge dark text into a dark cover or saturate bright highlights. Compare whole scenes and smaller regions rather than treating a stronger histogram spread as automatically better. This task uses a fixed pivot for every input, so there is no statistic fitted from training examples. A rule based on a dataset-derived mean would need that statistic estimated only from the training split and reused consistently later.

Try it

  1. Write the pivot and contrast factors explicitly.
  2. Apply the formula in float32 before clipping.
  3. Inspect shadows and highlights, not only the overall appearance.
Python · run in order
pivot = 127.5
factors = [0.6, 1.6]
contrasts = [np.rint(np.clip(pivot + a*(clean_rgb.astype(np.float32)-pivot),0,255)).astype(np.uint8) for a in factors]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
for ax, image, title in zip(axes, [clean_rgb]+contrasts, ['Original','Contrast 0.6','Contrast 1.6']):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis('off')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The reduced-contrast version moves toward the pivot. The increased-contrast version can look stronger while discarding distinctions near a storage limit.

Change and compare

  • Set the factor to one and verify identity after rounding.
  • Use pivot 100 with the same factor and compare the changed result.

Guided task 05

Power curves and gamma convention

A power curve changes intermediate values nonlinearly. First scale encoded RGB values into zero through one, then apply output = input ** gamma. In this lesson that is the exact exponent convention: gamma below one raises intermediate values and gamma above one lowers them. Some tools define their parameter as the reciprocal exponent, so always read the formula instead of guessing from the name.

The endpoints zero and one stay fixed for positive gamma. Values between them change smoothly and monotonically before rounding, but a uint8 result can still merge nearby inputs. The same channelwise curve is applied to red, green and blue. That is an appearance operation on encoded values; it is not the piecewise sRGB decoding function and does not create a linear-light radiometric representation. Show both the resulting images and the actual curves so the direction of the effect is unambiguous. Gamma adjustment cannot restore detail already removed by clipping or compression. Its usefulness for a later CNN depends on whether it preserves the evidence needed for the specific label.

Try it

  1. Scale RGB values to float32 in zero through one.
  2. Apply exponents 0.6 and 1.8 with the stated formula.
  3. Compare intermediate values and unchanged endpoints on the curves.
Python · run in order
unit_rgb = clean_rgb.astype(np.float32) / 255.0
gammas = [0.6, 1.8]
powered = [np.rint(np.clip(unit_rgb**g,0,1)*255).astype(np.uint8) for g in gammas]
axis_values = np.linspace(0,1,256)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.5))
for ax, image, title in zip(axes[:3], [clean_rgb]+powered, ['Original','Exponent 0.6','Exponent 1.8']):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis('off')
axes[3].plot(axis_values, axis_values, '--', label='Identity')
for g in gammas: axes[3].plot(axis_values, axis_values**g, label=f'Exponent {g}')
axes[3].set(xlabel='Encoded input / 255', ylabel='Encoded output / 255', title='Actual power curves', xlim=(0,1), ylim=(0,1))
axes[3].legend()
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Read the curves at the same input value. The upper curve produces the brighter intermediate value under this exponent convention, while both curves share the endpoints.

Change and compare

  • Try gamma one and confirm that the stored image is unchanged.
  • Compare the results of exponent 0.5 and exponent two on a value ramp.

Guided task 06

Global histogram equalization

Global histogram equalization builds a grayscale mapping from the distribution of values across the entire image. A cumulative-count-based mapping spreads occupied levels over the available output range. It is adaptive to each input image, unlike the fixed offset or fixed power curve used earlier. Identical input intensities within that image receive the same mapped output, even when they occur in different regions.

Equalization does not guarantee an exactly uniform output histogram. The input is discrete, several pixels can share one value, and a mapping cannot split those identical samples into different output levels. This task first compresses the grayscale drawing into a narrow interval, then compares equalization with that low-contrast input. The construction helps reveal the mechanism, but the earlier compression already rounded away some distinctions. Equalization cannot reconstruct those missing original levels. Nor does a wider distribution establish better performance on a future task. Inspect letters, smooth gradients and boundaries; an aggressive mapping can exaggerate weak background differences as well as useful detail.

Try it

  1. Compress grayscale values into a narrow interval.
  2. Apply equalizeHist to the single-channel uint8 image.
  3. Compare the images and their measured histograms.
Python · run in order
low_contrast = np.rint(80 + gray.astype(np.float32)*0.35).astype(np.uint8)
equalized = cv2.equalizeHist(low_contrast)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(low_contrast, cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=255)
axes[0].set_title('Narrow-range input')
axes[1].imshow(equalized, cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=255)
axes[1].set_title('Global equalization')
for ax in axes[:2]: ax.axis('off')
for image, label in [(low_contrast,'Input'),(equalized,'Equalized')]:
    axes[2].plot(np.bincount(image.ravel(),minlength=256), label=label)
axes[2].set(xlabel='Intensity',ylabel='Pixel count',xlim=(0,255),title='Actual distributions')
axes[2].legend()
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The equalized picture uses a broader range, but its histogram can still contain strong peaks and empty bins. Each output level is produced by a discrete mapping.

Change and compare

  • Compare equalization of the original gray image with this compressed case.
  • Count unique levels before and after; explain why a mapping cannot create distinctions between identical inputs.

Guided task 07

Local contrast with CLAHE

CLAHE applies contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization using a grid of local regions. Local distributions allow the adjustment to respond to different areas, while interpolation between mappings helps avoid hard seams. Contrast limiting restricts histogram amplification inside the algorithm. The clipLimit parameter is an algorithm setting, not a maximum allowed output intensity or a percentage of clipped image pixels.

OpenCV’s tileGridSize specifies the number of tiles along the horizontal and vertical directions, not the width and height of each tile in pixels. Smaller local regions can respond to smaller variations, which can also amplify texture or noise. We create a left-to-right shading field over the grayscale drawing and compare global equalization with a four-by-four tile grid. This field is a controlled drawing modification, not a calibrated model of a camera’s illumination. Keep the same zero-to-255 display range so automatic plot scaling does not hide tonal differences. Local enhancement can make a dark note more legible yet also reshape the background distribution. Review both effects before choosing settings for an input pipeline.

Try it

  1. Create a spatial shading field without changing the image coordinates.
  2. Compare global equalization with clipLimit 2 and a 4 by 4 tile grid.
  3. Inspect printed details and smooth regions with fixed display limits.
Python · run in order
shade = np.linspace(0.3,1.0,gray.shape[1],dtype=np.float32)[None,:]
shaded = np.rint(gray.astype(np.float32)*shade).astype(np.uint8)
global_shaded = cv2.equalizeHist(shaded)
clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0,tileGridSize=(4,4))
local_shaded = clahe.apply(shaded)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
for ax, image, title in zip(axes, [shaded,global_shaded,local_shaded], ['Uneven shading','Global mapping','CLAHE: 4 by 4 tiles']):
    ax.imshow(image,cmap='gray',vmin=0,vmax=255)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis('off')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Compare areas at both ends of the shading gradient. The local adjustment can behave differently across the image even for similar input intensities.

Change and compare

  • Compare tile grids 2 by 2 and 8 by 8 while keeping clipLimit fixed.
  • Try clipLimit one and four, inspecting background grain as well as text.

Guided task 08

Lightness adjustments and color tradeoffs

Applying a different histogram mapping independently to each RGB channel can change their relationships and visibly shift colors. A common alternative is to convert to a representation with a separate lightness channel, adjust that channel, and convert back. Here the uint8 OpenCV Lab representation stores a scaled L-star lightness channel alongside encoded a and b components. L-star is perceptual lightness; it should not be described as raw physical luminance.

Compare independent RGB equalization with CLAHE applied only to the Lab lightness channel. Holding the stored a and b values fixed avoids directly remapping them, but does not guarantee identical final RGB chromaticity or perceived color. Finite precision, conversion and output-gamut limits can still change the result. Keep the original beside both candidates and inspect the blue book, cream mug and yellow note separately. For a label that depends on color, those differences can invalidate an otherwise attractive preprocessing choice. For a reading target, legibility may be the more relevant criterion. This lesson produces inspectable candidates and documented rules; deciding whether to use one in a CNN requires a later controlled experiment with independent evaluation data.

Try it

  1. Equalize each RGB channel independently as a comparison candidate.
  2. Convert to Lab and apply CLAHE to the L channel only.
  3. Compare color relationships and small text in both results.
Python · run in order
independent_rgb = np.stack([cv2.equalizeHist(clean_rgb[...,c]) for c in range(3)],axis=-1)
lab_values = cv2.cvtColor(clean_rgb,cv2.COLOR_RGB2LAB)
adjusted_lab = lab_values.copy()
adjusted_lab[...,0] = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0,tileGridSize=(4,4)).apply(lab_values[...,0])
lightness_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(adjusted_lab,cv2.COLOR_LAB2RGB)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
for ax, image, title in zip(axes, [clean_rgb,independent_rgb,lightness_rgb], ['Original RGB','Independent RGB equalization','Lab lightness CLAHE']):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis('off')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The independent RGB mappings can strongly shift familiar colors. The lightness-only route also needs inspection; retaining two stored components is not a promise of unchanged displayed color.

Change and compare

  • Compare the note crop under both candidates.
  • Write a target label that would make a visible color shift unacceptable.
